facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus was an extinct genus of very small early crocodylomorphs measuring about 76 cm in length.
facts.quote: Terrestrisuchus is an extinct genus of very small early crocodylomorph that was about 76 cm long.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus had a short, shallow body with paired rows of osteoderms running from its neck down its back.
facts.quote: The body was relatively short and shallow, and the spine was topped by paired rows of osteoderms running down from its neck down its back.

facts.statement: The leaf-shaped osteoderms of Terrestrisuchus were longer than wide and featured a prominent front spur that slid under and interlocked with the scute in front of it.
facts.quote: These osteoderms are described as "leaf-shaped", being relatively longer than wide with a prominent spur at the front that slides under and interlocks with the scute in front of it.

facts.statement: The acetabulum of Terrestrisuchus is perforated, forming an opening between the hip bones.
facts.quote: The acetabulum (hip socket) of Terrestrisuchus is perforated and forms an opening between the hip bones.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus inhabited a chain of tropical, low-lying islands in southern Britain alongside small dinosaurs and abundant rhynchocephalians.
facts.quote: It inhabited a chain of tropical, low-lying islands that made up southern Britain, along with similarly small-sized dinosaurs and abundant rhynchocephalians.

facts.statement: The first fossils of Terrestrisuchus were discovered by Professor K. A. Kermack and Dr. Pamela Lamplugh Robinson in the spring of 1952 at the Pant-y-ffynon Quarry near Cowbridge, Glamorgan, South Wales.
facts.quote: The first fossils of Terrestrisuchus were discovered by Professor K. A. Kermack and Dr. Pamela Lamplugh Robinson in the spring of 1952, recovered from the Pant-y-ffynon Quarry located near Cowbridhe, Glamorgan in South Wales.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus was named and described by P. J. Crush in 1984, with the generic name emphasizing its terrestrial lifestyle and the specific name derived from the Latin word for its light, graceful build.
facts.quote: The specimens were eventually named and thoroughly described by P. J. Crush in 1984, with the generic name Terrestrisuchus chosen to emphasise the terrestrial lifestyle of this crocodylomorph, and the specific name from the Latin gracilis for its light, graceful build.

facts.statement: In 1984, Crush recognized Terrestrisuchus's close relationship to the German sphenosuchian Saltoposuchus and erected the family Saltoposuchidae for both genera.
facts.quote: When describing Terrestrisuchus in 1984, Crush recognised it shared a close relationship to the German "sphenosuchian", Saltoposuchus. As such, he erected the new family Saltoposuchidae for the two genera under "Sphenosuchia".

facts.statement: While Crush reconstructed Terrestrisuchus as a quadruped, subsequent studies have debated whether it may have been bipedal instead.
facts.quote: Crush reconstructed Terrestrisuchus as a quadruped, with noticeably longer hind limbs than its forelimbs and its hips held high above the shoulder. However, based on these proportions it has also been suggested that Terrestrisuchus may have been bipedal instead. This question remained controversial in subsequent studies.

facts.statement: The interlocking osteoderms provided rigid support for the body and limited spinal flexibility, aiding in supporting the body on land.
facts.quote: This provides a rigid support for the body and limited the flexibility of its spine, supporting its body on land.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus possessed tightly packed gastralia, or belly ribs.
facts.quote: Terrestrisuchus is also known to have had tightly packed gastralia, or belly ribs.

facts.statement: The genus Terrestrisuchus was formally described by P. J. Crush in 1984.
facts.quote: P. J. Crush. A late Upper Triassic sphenosuchid crocodilian from Wales. Palaeontology. 27 (1), s. 67–101, 1984.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Wales, United Kingdom.
facts.quote: Terrestrisuchus gracilis (gr. "cocodrilo terrestre") es un género extinto de cocodrilomorfo esfenosuquio de la familia Saltoposuchidae que vivió hacia finales del Triásico en lo que hoy es Gales (Reino Unido).

facts.statement: The authority for the genus Terrestrisuchus is attributed to Crush, 1984.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Crush, 1984

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus was a slender animal with stylized legs.
facts.quote: Este antecesor de los cocodrilos actuales era mucho más delgado y sus patas eran estilizadas.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus had an extremely long tail that added about 50 cm to its length.
facts.quote: Otra característica era su larguísima cola, con la que sumaba unos 50 cm.

facts.statement: Experts believe Terrestrisuchus was likely terrestrial and fast, feeding on small prey such as insects due to its size.
facts.quote: Era muy probablemente terrestre (y veloz), y su dieta se basaba en pequeñas presas como insectos, según creen los expertos, debido a su tamaño.

facts.statement: Although Terrestrisuchus did not look like a crocodile at first glance, its skull was very similar to that of crocodiles.
facts.quote: Aunque el Terrestrisuchus no parecía un cocodrilo a simple vista, su cráneo es muy similar a los de estos animales.

facts.statement: A 2013 re-evaluation concluded that evidence supported Terrestrisuchus as a distinct genus rather than a synonym of Saltoposuchus.
facts.quote: A formal re-evaluation of the hypothesis in 2013 concluded that the available evidence was not consistent with the two species being synonymous, and that it is likely that Terrestrisuchus is indeed its own genus.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus was a coastal species, which is unusual for basal crocodylomorphs typically found in inland floodplains.
facts.quote: Terrestrisuchus was a coastal species, unusual for basal crocodylomorphs, which are typically known from inland floodplain environments.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus likely inhabited forested karstic environments with fissures and sinkholes eroded into limestone.
facts.quote: The islands were forested karstic environments, riddled with fissures, sinkholes and caverns eroded into the limestone, environments which long limbed, agile reptiles like Terrestrisuchus may have been well suited to inhabit.

facts.statement: Abundant rhynchocephalians, including Clevosaurus cambrica, likely formed a large part of Terrestrisuchus's diet, possibly evidenced by bite marks on their bones.
facts.quote: Rhynchocephalians (relatives of modern tuataras) were very abundant and are known from at least three species including Clevosaurus cambrica, Diphydontosaurus and at least one or two unnamed species, which likely formed a large part of the diet of Terrestrisuchus (possibly evidenced by bite marks on the bones of Clevosaurus that likely belong to Terrestrisuchus).

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus had thin, serrated teeth indicating it was a carnivorous generalist pursuit hunter of small to mid-sized prey.
facts.quote: The thin, serrated teeth of Terrestrisuchus indicate that it was carnivorous, and like other early crocodylomorphs it was likely a generalist pursuit hunter that preyed upon small to mid-sized prey items.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus had rigidly sutured hip bones with an elongated, non-mobile pubis, unlike modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: The shape and construction of its hip bones, particularly the elongated pubis, indicate that they were rigidly sutured together and that its pubis was not mobile as it is in modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus likely did not use the hepatic piston breathing method found in modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: This indicates that Terrestrisuchus would not have utilised the hepatic piston method of breathing found in modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: The dimensions of Terrestrisuchus's orbit and scleral ring suggest it was a cathemeral animal.
facts.quote: Also, the dimensions of its orbit and scleral ring suggest that it was a cathemeral animal.

facts.statement: Microstructure of Terrestrisuchus limb bones indicates a relatively fast growth rate compared to other archosauriforms and pseudosuchians.
facts.quote: The microstructure of the limb bones of Terrestrisuchus show that it was well vascularised and contained large amounts of energy-consuming fibrolamellar bone tissue, indicating a relatively fast growth-rate for Terrestrisuchus compared to other archosauriforms and even other pseudosuchians.

facts.statement: Terrestrisuchus lived from 237 to 227.3 million years ago during the Carnian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Carnian to Carnian (237 to 227.3 million years ago)
